title: What’s the Matter With the Democratic Party?
author: Geoff Shullenberger
content:
![What’s the Matter With the Democratic
Party?](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-29-at-10.48.27
---PM.png)

> _Nothing Left: Confessions of a Democratic Operative_  
>  By Evan Barker  
> Threshold, 288 pages, $29

In the summer of 2004, as the Democratic Party hurtled toward its second
defeat at the hands of George W. Bush, the Kansas City-born historian and
writer Thomas Frank published _What 's the Matter With Kansas?_ Frank's basic
thesis--that Republicans had used culture-war wedge issues to get working-
class voters to back an economic agenda unfavorable to their interests--seemed
to be vindicated by Bush's victory. It was widely reported, after all, that
Karl Rove's strategy of using state-level referenda on gay marriage to drive
turnout for Bush had been a decisive factor in the outcome. Frank's book
became a sensation, and spent months on the _Times_ bestseller list.

> "Frank's real target was the Democratic Party."

Today, _What 's the Matter With Kansas?_ often seems to be misremembered as a
coastal liberal lament about the benighted heartland. But Frank's real target
was the Democratic Party, which he argued had sold out its one-time base in
favor of the donor class and ceased to even try to channel the concerns of
average voters across much of the country. As Frank summarized his position in
a 2006 column: "Democratic leaders must learn to talk about class issues
again."

Frank's follow-up book, _Listen, Liberal_ , put this critique of the Democrats
front and center, contending that the party had become "the party of the
professional class," to its detriment. One reviewer proposed its title should
have been "What's the Matter With Massachusetts?" _Listen, Liberal_ was
released in the spring of another election year that would prove disastrous
for Democrats: 2016. In the intervening years, Barack Obama's two commanding
victories might have seemed to invalidate Frank's gloomy earlier prognosis
that the party would see its "relevance slowly ebbing." But he argued that
Obama had squandered the populist moment that followed the 2008 crash, and
that Democrats would pay the price. During that election cycle, Frank backed
Bernie Sanders, and was among the few left-of-center pundits who didn't doubt
Trump could actually win.

Ten years after _Listen, Liberal_ , another native of the Kansas City area has
published a similarly themed indictment of the Democratic Party. The author of
this new _cri de coeur_ , the former Democratic fundraiser and operative Evan
Barker, tells us she became disillusioned with the party upon realizing that
"the Democrats were now run by people who had zero cultural connection to the
people the party had long represented." Although she had inklings of this for
years while ensconced inside the party's machinery, the scales finally fell
from her eyes during Kamala Harris's coronation at the party's 2024 National
Convention.

Eight years prior to that, Frank had denounced the Democrats for having
severed their "bonds to working people," and decried a party that "dedicates
itself to the concerns of a particular slice of high-achieving affluent
people." But it was around this time that the now disillusioned Barker was
first immersing herself in campaign work. She was driven, as she tells it, by
gratitude that Obamacare had given her access to healthcare despite a severe
chronic illness, and by a desire to fight for the interests of her working-
class family in Kansas and Missouri.

Although she launched her career as part of the Clinton campaign, Barker soon
became a dogged opponent of the centrist establishment, employed in the
network of insurgent electoral projects that grew out of Bernie Sanders's 2016
challenge to Clinton. After a brief and ill-fated stint working for a suburban
Clintonite girlboss running for Congress in New Jersey, she moved on to the
campaign of Brent Welder, a Sanders-aligned progressive upstart in her native
Kansas who later lost the primary to the establishment-backed Sharice Davids.
In this race, the establishment strategically deployed Davids's identity as a
Native American lesbian as a cudgel against the white male Welder--and
succeeded. (Clinton ran a similar playbook against Sanders.) In Barker's
telling, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who had just won her primary upset against
Joe Crowley, hesitated to endorse Welder, saying she didn't "want to be seen
as someone who isn't supporting another woman of color." But in the end, "AOC
put the Bernie Bros first."

That might have seemed encouraging, but shouldn't have been. Not only did
Welder lose, the progressive wing of the Democrats proved just as fixated on
identity as the establishment. Moreover, Barker argues, "both wings captured
each other's worst impulses": The party's left flank leaned into ever more
radical rhetoric on race and gender, and got the party's mainstream to go
along with it while downplaying policies like Medicare for All. The "merger"
of insurgents and insiders symbolized by the 2019 _Rolling Stone_ cover
featuring AOC and Nancy Pelosi, according to Barker, "came at the expense of
the populist vision expressed in Bernie's 2016 campaign." The terms of the
pact dictated that "the party would only focus on the culture war."

Here one might notice an echo of Frank's thesis in _What 's the Matter With
Kansas?_--but now it is the Democrats who are using "culture war" as a
diversion from material politics. Cultural conditions had changed considerably
in the meantime, though. In the 2000s, Frank had evidently assumed that
abortion and gay marriage were and would remain losing issues for Democrats to
foreground. But especially after _Obergefell_ seemed to portend the inexorable
advance of cultural progressivism, it became possible to imagine the opposite
was true. Leaning left on the culture war could therefore become the main
thing uniting progressive and centrist Democrats.

Nearly a decade on, the political valence of culture war issues seems in flux
again, even as what exactly those issues are has also shifted. Barker
concludes her book, in part, by calling for "moderation" on this front from
both parties, but what that means can be difficult to parse. After
facilitating the apparent pro-life triumph of the _Dobbs_ decision, Donald
Trump has often been concerned to present himself as a moderate on abortion,
but he has no such compunctions when it comes to transgender issues.
Moderation in 2026 means something different than it did in 2016 in part
because the cultural ground has shifted, as it will continue to do. The
problem with the "moderate" position is that it is often little more than a
lagging indicator of such changes.

* * *

What is most valuable about _Nothing Left_ is that Barker was on the inside of
the effort to push the Democrats in a left-populist direction, roughly along
the lines Frank argued for. She rubbed shoulders with Sanders as well as AOC,
compared notes with the founders of Justice Democrats, and was employed by the
fundraising outfit Left Rising, which assisted the rise of figures like Summer
Lee and Cori Bush. By her account, this tendency only succeeded by betraying
its original impetus. Its efforts, Barker concludes, only deepened the party's
disconnect with working-class voters.

> "This tendency only succeeded by betraying its original impetus."

Barker traded in her career as a behind-the-scenes operative for that of a
public-facing pundit with a viral TikTok video posted after the Harris
coronation, in which she denounced the party's disastrous trajectory. Later
that year, as she [_recounted_](https://www.thefp.com/p/democrat-fundraiser-
evan-barker-i-voted-trump?ref=compactmag.com) in an essay for _The Free Press_
, she voted for Donald Trump, an act she presented there and continues to
present in the book as more of a protest vote than a full-bore endorsement of
the MAGA project. "My vote for Trump," she writes in _Nothing Left_ , "made me
a conscientious objector in the wars of our politics."

Even if she voted for Trump in uncompetitive California, it seems questionable
to present a vote for one candidate as equivalent to the rejection of both.
Elsewhere, Barker says that at the time of Trump's 2024 victory she had "hoped
for a true realignment" by which the GOP would "become the true party of the
working class." She expresses disappointment that Trump has instead "cut
social safety net programs, defunded healthcare, and started new wars."

Nonetheless, these actions seem to be less viscerally objectionable to Barker
than the cultural ambience she was exposed to in Democratic circles. What
evidently soured her on her former party was its insiders' repugnant cocktail
of viciousness, cynicism, and identitarian self-righteousness. The reaction is
entirely understandable, but it also ratifies an insight Barker would like, in
theory, to reject: that the animal spirits of culture war enjoy more potency
than alternative sources of political identity and commitment.

Barker's own recent career path offers further proof of this unpleasant truth.
Although she underlines her continued independence from the Republican Party,
she is now de facto ensconced in the conservative media ecosystem. _Nothing
Left_ is published by an imprint whose other authors include Glenn Beck, Greg
Abbott, Pete Hegseth, and Donald Trump himself. Far be it from me--a non-
right-wing author with plenty of bylines in right-wing outlets--to fault
Barker for any of that. But her apparent value in this context tells us that
the Republican coalition remains adept at playing on (often enough reasonable)
cultural antipathies to compensate for the dismal reality of its material
project. As Frank put it in _What 's the Matter With Kansas?_: "The trick
never ages: ... Vote to strike a blow against elitism; receive a social order
in which wealth is more concentrated than ever before in our lifetimes, in
which workers have been stripped of power and CEOs are rewarded in a manner
beyond imagining."
